semantic_correction.stem: Which technique should a client use when instilling prescribed eye drops?

options.A: Pull the upper eyelid upward and place the bottle tip against the eye surface so the prescribed drop reaches the cornea without missing the target.
options.B: Close the eye first and place the prescribed drop on the eyelid margin, then blink repeatedly so the medication moves into the eye from the lashes.
options.C: Pull the lower eyelid down to form a pocket, instill the prescribed drops into the pocket, and keep the bottle tip from touching the eye, eyelid, or hands.
options.D: Instill the prescribed drop directly onto the center of the cornea, then rub the closed eye to spread the medication across the ocular surface.

semantic_correction.rationale: C is correct. Current National Eye Institute guidance instructs patients to tilt the head back, pull the lower eyelid down and away from the eyeball to form a pocket, hold the bottle tip just above that pocket, and squeeze the prescribed number of drops into it. NEI also advises washing the hands before use and preventing the bottle tip from touching the hands, eye, or eyelid to reduce contamination risk. Therefore the safest technique is to instill the drops into the lower conjunctival pocket without contact between the bottle tip and the eye or eyelid. A is incorrect because touching the bottle tip to the ocular surface can contaminate the bottle and injure the eye. B is incorrect because placing medication on the closed eyelid does not follow the recommended instillation technique. D is incorrect because drops should be placed in the lower-eyelid pocket rather than directly on the cornea, and vigorous rubbing is not part of the recommended technique.
semantic_correction.educational_objective: Demonstrate safe ophthalmic medication administration by placing prescribed drops into the lower conjunctival pocket while preventing contact between the bottle tip and the eye, eyelid, or hands.

audit_findings_append.finding: The revised item tests safe ophthalmic drop instillation with one clearly best technique, balanced alternatives, current NEI guidance, and no answer-length cue.

option_audit.A: Incorrect. The bottle tip should not touch the eye or eyelid, and the recommended target is the lower-eyelid pocket rather than direct corneal contact.
option_audit.B: Incorrect. NEI instructs clients to create a lower-eyelid pocket and instill the drops into it rather than placing medication on a closed eyelid.
option_audit.C: Correct. It directly matches NEI technique and contamination-prevention instructions.
option_audit.D: Incorrect. Direct corneal instillation and rubbing do not match the recommended technique and may cause discomfort or contamination.

ambiguity_check: No second defensible answer. C uniquely combines the correct lower-pocket target and no-touch technique; A and D use direct ocular contact/corneal delivery, and B places the medication outside the conjunctival pocket.
cueing_check: All four options are parallel eye-drop administration techniques of comparable length and specificity; the prior uniquely-long correct response was removed.
